summary: This proposed standard specifies multilateral interconnection at Internet Exchange Points, where three or more BGP speakers exchange routing information through a single intermediary called a route server. The document describes how a route server should behave so participants need fewer individual sessions with one another.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7947 describes the route server, the middleman at an Internet exchange point that passes routing information between participants. Instead of every participant having a direct session with every other one, each one tells the route server what it can reach, and the route server tells the others. The route server never carries the traffic, and it leaves the routing attributes alone so that each participant keeps control of its own policy.

subtitle: How a route server lets many networks at an exchange point share routes through one broker instead of a full mesh of sessions.

tldr.problem: At a large Internet exchange point, every participant that wants to reach every other participant would need a BGP session with each of them, and that overhead does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: A route server brokers reachability information: each participant announces its routes to the route server over EBGP, and the route server forwards them to the other participants with the well-known attributes left unchanged, so that each participant's own routing policy still decides what to accept.
tldr.outcome: Participants need one session instead of many, and the route server stays out of the data path. The RFC also explains the one known drawback of per-client filtering on a route server, known as path hiding, and two ways to avoid it.

today: RFC 7947 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It describes the behaviour of a BGP route server, and it refers to RFC 7948 for the recommendations on operating one.

sections.title: Multilateral Interconnection and the Route Server
sections.content:
Internet Exchange Points provide IP data interconnection facilities for their participants, typically over shared Layer 2 media such as Ethernet. The Border Gateway Protocol, an inter-Autonomous System routing protocol, is commonly used to exchange network reachability information over such media.

Bilateral EBGP sessions between exchange participants used to be the most common way of exchanging reachability information, but the overhead of dense interconnection causes substantial operational scaling problems for participants of larger exchange points. Multilateral interconnection replaces those sessions with a third-party brokering system, commonly called a route server and typically managed by the exchange operator. Each participant, usually called a route server client, announces its reachability information to the route server using EBGP, and the route server forwards it to each connected client according to its configuration.

Although the route server uses BGP to exchange information with its clients, it does not forward traffic itself and is therefore not a router. It can be seen as similar in function to a route reflector, except that it operates using EBGP instead of Internal BGP. Certain adaptions to RFC 4271 are needed to make an EBGP router behave as a route server, and those adaptions are the subject of Section 2. Route server functionality is not mandatory in BGP implementations.

The RFC uses the term route server only for multilateral peering brokerage. The same word is also used for a different kind of system: a BGP node that accepts feeds from multiple clients for operational analysis and troubleshooting, also called a route collector or a route-views server.
sections.plainLanguage: An Internet exchange point is where networks meet to exchange traffic. The usual arrangement is that each network has a direct routing session with every other network there, which works fine for a handful of participants and becomes unwieldy for dozens. A route server sits in the middle: every participant has one session with it, and it passes the routing information along. It never carries the traffic itself.

sections.title: Accepting Routes and Choosing What to Send
sections.content:
A route server must accept all UPDATE messages received from each of its clients for inclusion in its Adj-RIB-In. Those UPDATE messages may then be omitted from the route server's Loc-RIB, or from its Loc-RIBs, because of filters configured to implement routing policy. The route server should perform one or more BGP Decision Processes to select routes for later advertisement to its clients, taking into account any configuration that provides multiple paths to a particular client or multiple Loc-RIBs. It should then forward UPDATE messages from its Loc-RIB or Loc-RIBs to its clients as determined by local policy.

In other words, the route server keeps everything it is told, but what it actually advertises to each client is a matter of the operator's filtering configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: The route server takes in every route announcement it receives and keeps a copy. Whether a given route is passed on to a particular participant is decided by filters set up by the exchange operator, not by the route server making a fresh routing decision on the participant's behalf.

sections.title: Leaving the Routing Attributes Alone
sections.content:
A route server mainly brokers, and changing attributes could cause clients to change their own BGP Decision Process and so alter the intended routing policies of the exchange participants. For that reason, contrary to what RFC 4271 specifies, route servers should not by default update well-known attributes received from clients before redistributing them to the other clients, unless explicitly configured to do so. Optional attributes, whether recognised or not and whether transitive or not, should also not be updated, unless local operator configuration enforces it, and should be passed on to the other clients.

Four attributes are called out. NEXT_HOP defines the IP address of the router used as the next hop to the destinations in the UPDATE message. Because the route server does not take part in routing traffic, the NEXT_HOP attribute must be passed unmodified to the clients, like the third-party next hop feature of RFC 4271.

AS_PATH identifies the autonomous systems through which the routing information has passed. Since the route server does not forward data between clients, and since modifying AS_PATH could affect the client's decision process, the route server should not prepend its own AS number nor modify the AS_PATH segment in any other way. This differs from RFC 4271, which requires a BGP speaker to prepend its own AS number as the last element of the AS_PATH segment. It is a recommendation rather than a requirement, so that legacy clients which do not yet support the client-side rule below keep working.

On the client side, a route server client must be able to accept UPDATE messages where the leftmost AS in the AS_PATH is not the AS number of the route server that sent it. If the client's BGP implementation has a check for this, the implementation must allow the check to be disabled, and should allow it to be disabled per peer.

MULTI_EXIT_DISC is an optional non-transitive attribute used on external links to discriminate among multiple exit or entry points to the same neighbouring autonomous system. Contrary to RFC 4271, when it is applied to an NLRI UPDATE sent to a route server, it should be propagated to the other clients and the route server should not modify its value.

Communities and Extended Communities label information carried in UPDATE messages. Transitive and non-transitive Communities attributes applied to an NLRI UPDATE sent to a route server should not be modified, processed or removed, except as defined by local policy. If a Communities attribute is meant for the route server itself, as local policy determines, it may be modified or removed.
sections.plainLanguage: The route server passes attributes through rather than rewriting them, because rewriting them would change what other participants think they are agreeing to. Two things follow: the route server does not add its own autonomous system number to the path, and the receiving side must be able to accept a message whose leftmost autonomous system is not the route server's own.

sections.title: Per-Client Filtering and Path Hiding
sections.content:
Participants often use route servers in order to interconnect with as many other participants as possible, but there are circumstances where control of path distribution per client matters, to ensure that desired interconnection policies are met. That control can lead to a path being hidden from a client, which the RFC calls path hiding. Section 2.3 and its subsections are informational and do not form part of the normative specification.

In the traditional bilateral model, per-client policy control towards another participant is done either by not having a bilateral interconnection with it or by filtering outbound on the BGP session towards it. In a multilateral environment only the route server can filter outbound towards a client, so clients depend on the route server to do their outbound filtering for them.

Assuming the BGP Decision Process is used, when the same prefix is advertised to the route server from several clients the route server selects a single path for propagation to all connected clients. If the route server is configured to filter that calculated best path from reaching a particular client, that client receives no path for the prefix, even though other paths the route server received might have been policy compliant for that client. The RFC's example: the same prefix is sent to the route server via AS2 and via AS4, the route via AS2 is preferred by the decision process, and AS2's policy prevents the route server from sending that path to AS1. AS1 then never receives a path to the prefix, even though a valid alternative path via AS4 had been received. This happens because the decision process is performed only once, on the route server, for all clients.

Path hiding only occurs on route servers that employ per-client policy control. An exchange operator that deploys a route server without a per-client routing policy control system does not get path hiding, because all paths are considered equally valid from the route server's point of view.
sections.plainLanguage: Filtering routes per client has a side effect. The route server picks one best path for a prefix and offers it to everyone; if that path is then withheld from one client, that client gets nothing, even though a second path it would have accepted is sitting in the route server. The client loses a route it could have used.

sections.title: Avoiding Path Hiding
sections.content:
Three approaches avoid path hiding.

The most portable is to use a route server implementation that performs the per-client best path calculation for each set of paths to a prefix, after the client policies have been taken into account. This can be done with per-client Loc-RIBs, with path filtering between the Adj-RIB-In and each per-client Loc-RIB. An implementation can optimise this by keeping unfiltered paths in a global Loc-RIB and storing the per-client Loc-RIBs as deltas against it. The approach is highly portable because it makes no assumption about what the clients can do.

The second approach assumes the route server can send more than one path for a prefix to a client, which would remove the dependency on a single path and with it the path hiding problem. The diverse BGP path proposal of RFC 6774 does this with a separate BGP session from the route server to a client for each different path. The number of paths that can be distributed is limited by the number of sessions the two sides are willing to establish, so the method is not guaranteed to eliminate path hiding in every situation, and it may significantly increase the number of BGP sessions the route server handles, which can hurt its performance.

The third approach uses the ADD-PATH mechanism of RFC 7911, which lets a BGP speaker forward multiple paths for the same prefix on a single session. Because RFC 4271 requires a BGP listener to implement an implicit withdraw when it receives an UPDATE for a prefix that already exists in its Adj-RIB-In, this needs explicit support on both the route server and its clients. If ADD-PATH is negotiated bidirectionally and the client propagates several paths for the same prefix to the route server, that could cause inactive, invalid or suboptimal paths to reach the route server and cost other clients reachability. For that reason, ADD-PATH on a route server should be enforced in a send-only mode with the clients, which results in negotiating a receive-only mode from the client towards the route server.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to avoid losing a route that a client would have accepted. The route server can run a separate best-path calculation per client. It can open a second session to the client for each extra path. Or it can use the ADD-PATH extension to send several paths on one session, but only in the direction of the client, so that clients cannot push bad paths back at the route server.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The path hiding problem can, in certain circumstances, be used to proactively block third-party path announcements from other route server clients. Route server operators should be aware that security issues may arise unless steps are taken to mitigate path hiding.

The AS_PATH check described in Section 2.2.2 is normally enabled to check for malformed AS paths. If it is disabled, the client loses the ability to check incoming UPDATE messages for certain categories of problem, which could cause corrupted UPDATE messages to be propagated where they would not otherwise have been. The check is also used to detect BGP loops, so removing it could cause routing loops to form. It should therefore not be disabled by exchange participants unless it is needed to establish BGP sessions with a route server, and if possible should be disabled only for peers that are route servers.

Route server operators should also consider the security practices discussed in RFC 7454, BGP Operations and Security.
sections.plainLanguage: Path hiding is not only a routing inconvenience: a participant can use it to block announcements that other participants made, without the route server operator doing anything wrong. That is why the RFC asks for the checks that catch malformed paths and routing loops to stay switched on, and to be disabled only where a route server makes them impossible to keep.

items.title: Per-client Loc-RIBs
items.text: Run the best path calculation once per client, after filtering, and keep a global Loc-RIB with per-client deltas.

items.title: Diverse BGP paths
items.text: Use one extra BGP session per path. Limited by how many sessions both sides will run.

items.title: ADD-PATH, send-only
items.text: Send several paths on one session, but negotiate receive-only towards the route server.
